items.summary: Finding 1 (authors' own heading): in-domain performance is not a good indicator of out-of-domain generalization; BM25 underperforms neural approaches by 7-18 points in-domain yet is a strong OOD baseline.
items.conditions: comparison of Table 2's MS MARCO column against its Avg.-vs-BM25 row
items.notes: 'We observe BM25 heavily underperforms neural approaches by 7-18 points on in-domain MS MARCO. However, BEIR reveals it to be a strong baseline for generalization and generally outperforming many other, more complex approaches. This stresses the point, that retrieval methods must be evaluated on a broad range of datasets.'

items.summary: Finding 2: term-weighting sparse methods (DeepCT, SPARTA) fail to generalize despite strong in-domain MS MARCO scores; document-expansion (docT5query) generalizes better, beating BM25 on 11/18 datasets.
items.conditions: across 18 BEIR datasets
items.notes: '...they completely fail to generalize well by under performing BM25 on nearly all datasets. In contrast, document expansion based docT5query is able to add new relevant keywords to a document and performs strong on the BEIR datasets. It outperforms BM25 on 11/18 datasets while providing a competitive performance on the remaining datasets.'

items.summary: Finding 3: dense bi-encoder retrievers show issues generalizing out-of-distribution; DPR (the only system not trained on MS MARCO) generalizes worst overall.
items.conditions: across 18 BEIR datasets, esp. BioASQ (domain shift) and Touché-2020 (task shift)
items.notes: 'Dense retrieval models (esp. ANCE and TAS-B)... perform strongly on certain datasets, while on many other datasets perform significantly worse than BM25... dense retrievers are observed to underperform on datasets with a large domain shift... like in BioASQ, or task-shifts like in Touché-2020. DPR, the only non-MSMARCO trained dataset overall performs the worst in generalization on the benchmark.'

items.summary: Finding 4: re-ranking (BM25+CE) and late-interaction (ColBERT) generalize best out-of-distribution; BM25+CE beats BM25 on 16/18 datasets (fails only on ArguAna and Touché-2020); ColBERT beats BM25 on 9/18.
items.conditions: across 18 BEIR datasets
items.notes: 'The cross-attentional re-ranking model (BM25+CE) performs the best and is able to outperform BM25 on almost all (16/18) datasets. It only fails on ArguAna and Touché-2020, two retrieval tasks that are extremely different to the MS MARCO training dataset... ColBERT... is still able to outperform BM25 on 9/18 datasets. It appears that cross-attention and cross-attentional like operations are important for a good out-of-distribution generalization.'

items.summary: Finding 5: TAS-B gives the best zero-shot generalization among the dense models tested, beating ANCE on 14/18 and DPR on 17/18 datasets; the authors speculate this reflects its training setup.
items.conditions: across 18 BEIR datasets
items.notes: 'TAS-B provides the best zero-shot generalization performance among its dense counterparts. It outperforms ANCE on 14/18 and DPR on 17/18 datasets respectively. We speculate that the reason lies in a strong training setup in combination of both in-domain batch negatives and Margin-MSE losses for the TAS-B model. This training loss function (with strong ensemble teachers in a Knowledge Distillation setup) shows strong generalization performances.'

items.summary: Finding 6: TAS-B underperforms ANCE on TREC-COVID (by 17.3 points) and Touché-2020 (by 7.8 points); the two models retrieve documents of very different median length on these datasets.
items.conditions: top-10 retrieved documents, nDCG@10, per dataset
items.notes: 'TAS-B underperforms ANCE on two datasets: TREC-COVID by 17.3 points and Touché-2020 by 7.8 points... On TREC-COVID, TAS-B retrieves documents with a median length of mere 10 words versus ANCE with 160 words. Similarly on Touché-2020, 14 words vs. 89 words with TAS-B and ANCE respectively.'

items.summary: Finding 7: GenQ (TAS-B further fine-tuned on synthetic in-domain queries) outperforms TAS-B on specialized domains (science, finance, community Q&A) but underperforms TAS-B on broader, more generic domains such as Wikipedia.
items.conditions: per-domain comparison, GenQ vs. TAS-B
items.notes: 'It outperforms the TAS-B model on specialized domains like scientific publications, finance or StackExchange. On broader and more generic domains, like Wikipedia, it performs weaker than the original TAS-B model.'

items.summary: Authors' stated motivation for building BEIR.
items.notes: 'So far, it is unclear how well existing trained neural models will perform for other text domains or textual retrieval tasks. Even more important, it is unclear how well different approaches, like sparse embeddings vs. dense embeddings, generalize to out-of-distribution data.'

items.summary: Authors' stated rationale for the dataset/task selection criteria used to assemble BEIR.
items.notes: 'the methodology is motivated by the following ... factors: (i) Diverse tasks... (ii) Diverse domains... (iii) Task difficulties... If a task is easily solved by any algorithm, it will not be useful to compare various models... (iv) Diverse annotation strategies: Creating retrieval datasets are inherently complex and are subject to annotation biases... To reduce the impact of such biases, we selected datasets which have been created in many different ways.' NB: the source text says 'three factors' but enumerates four (i)-(iv); quoted verbatim, discrepancy not resolved by the source.

items.summary: Authors' stated rationale for choosing nDCG@10 as the single evaluation metric across all BEIR tasks.
items.notes: 'Decision support metrics such as Precision and Recall which are both rank unaware are not suitable. Binary rank-aware metrics such as MRR... and MAP... fail to evaluate tasks with graded relevance judgements. We find that Normalised Cumulative Discount Gain (nDCG@k) provides a good balance suitable for both tasks involving binary and graded relevance judgements.'

items.summary: BM25 configuration used (Anserini, default Lucene parameters), with the authors' note that this was found to perform best among the options they tried.
items.notes: 'We use Anserini with the default Lucene parameters (k=0.9 and b=0.4)... In our leaderboard, we also tested Elasticsearch BM25 and Anserini + RM3 expansion, but found Anserini BM25 to perform the best.' Recorded as method_detail (not rationale_stated) since it is a minor implementation parameter choice, not elevated to a tracked Introduction/Methods rationale claim -- see state.json accepted-risk on rationale-claim scope.

items.summary: All neural architectures truncate documents to the first 512 word pieces because of the input-length limits of transformer encoders.
items.conditions: applies to all neural (sparse/dense/late-interaction/re-ranking) systems, all datasets
items.notes: 'Due to the length limitations of transformer-based networks, we use only the first 512 word pieces within all documents in our experiments across all neural architectures.'

items.summary: GenQ implementation: T5-base fine-tuned on MS MARCO for 2 epochs, then 5 synthetic queries generated per target document (top-k=25, top-p=0.95); TAS-B is further fine-tuned on the synthetic query-document pairs with in-batch negatives; target documents per dataset capped at 100K for resource reasons; GenQ trains an independent model per task.
items.notes: 'Due to resource constraints, we cap the maximum number of target documents in each dataset to 100K.'

items.summary: DeepCT is combined with BM25 using default Anserini parameters rather than parameters re-tuned for MS MARCO, because the authors empirically found this performed better.
items.notes: 'We use the original setup of Dai and Callan in combination with BM25 with default Anserini parameters which we empirically found to perform better over the tuned MS MARCO parameters.'

items.summary: SPARTA was re-implemented from scratch because the original implementation was not publicly available (DistilBERT fine-tuned on MS MARCO, 2,000 non-zero sparse dimensions); docT5query replicates a published setup, generating 40 queries per document.
Model/training details for DPR, ANCE, TAS-B, ColBERT, and BM25+CE as evaluated in BEIR.

value.DPR: bert-base-uncased bi-encoder, one BM25 hard negative + in-batch negatives, trained on NQ+TriviaQA+WebQuestions+CuratedTREC ('Multi' checkpoint)
value.ANCE: RoBERTa bi-encoder with ANN-mined hard negatives, MS MARCO, 600K steps
value.TAS-B: bi-encoder, Balanced Topic-Aware Sampling, Margin-MSE + in-batch negative loss, distilled from a cross-encoder/ColBERT ensemble
value.ColBERT: bert-base-uncased, max sequence length 300, MS MARCO 300K steps; end-to-end retrieval via faiss ANN (depth=100) then late-interaction re-ranking
value.BM25+CE: 6-layer 384-hidden MiniLM cross-encoder re-ranking BM25's top-100, trained on MS MARCO via knowledge distillation from an ensemble of BERT-base, BERT-large and ALBERT-large teachers; selected as best of 14 public cross-encoders tested

items.summary: Domain-overlap analysis (pairwise weighted Jaccard similarity on unigram word overlap, Figure 2) shows relatively low overlap across BEIR's different domains.
items.conditions: pairwise across all 18 BEIR datasets
items.notes: 'From Figure 2, we observe a rather low weighted Jaccard word overlap across different domains, indicating that BEIR is a challenging benchmark where approaches must generalize well to diverse out-of-distribution domains.'

items.summary: Controlled ablation (Appendix H): two distilbert-base-uncased models trained identically on MS MARCO, differing only in similarity function (cosine vs. dot-product).
items.conditions: identical architecture (distilbert-base-uncased), training data (MS MARCO), and loss (InfoNCE with in-batch negatives); only the similarity function varied
items.notes: 'We trained two distilbert-base-uncased models with an identical training setup on MS MARCO... and only changed the similarity function from cosine-similarity to dot-product... For TREC-COVID, the dot-product model achieves the biggest improvement with 15.3 points.'

items.summary: The cosine-similarity model in the Appendix H ablation systematically retrieves shorter documents (e.g. title-only papers) while the dot-product model retrieves longer ones, because dot-product magnitude scales with vector/document length while cosine similarity does not.
items.conditions: same ablation as E027
items.notes: 'Cosine-similarity uses vectors of unit length, thereby having no notion of the encoded text length. In contrast, for dot-product, longer documents result in vectors with higher magnitudes which can yield higher similarity scores for a query.'

items.summary: Relevance is not uniformly distributed over document length across datasets (Figure 5): for Touché-2020, longer documents are disproportionately annotated as highly relevant.
items.conditions: Touché-2020, original relevant-document length distribution
items.notes: 'relevance judgement scores are not uniformly distributed over document lengths: for some datasets, longer documents are annotated with higher relevancy scores, while in others, shorter documents are.'

items.summary: Author-stated limitation (Appendix B, item 1): BEIR currently covers English only.
items.notes: 'Although we aim for a diverse retrieval evaluation benchmark, due to the limited availability of multilingual retrieval datasets, all datasets covered in the BEIR benchmark are currently English... Future work could include multi- and cross-lingual tasks and models.'

items.summary: Author-stated limitation (Appendix B, item 2): long-document retrieval is not well covered, constrained by the 512-word-piece limit of transformer models.
items.notes: 'Most of our tasks have average document lengths up-to a few hundred words... Including tasks that require the retrieval of longer documents would be highly relevant. However, as transformer-based approaches often have a length limit of 512 word pieces, a fundamentally different setup would be required.'

items.summary: Author-stated limitation (Appendix B, item 3): BEIR evaluates pure textual search only, without auxiliary ranking signals used in real applications.
items.notes: 'Until now, we focused on pure textual search in BEIR. In many real-world applications, further signals are used to estimate the relevancy of documents, such as PageRank, recency, authority score or user-interactions such as click-through rates. The integration of such signals... is often not straight-forward and is an interesting direction for research.'

items.summary: Author-stated limitation (Appendix B, item 4): BEIR retrieves over only one or two document fields, even though real documents often have several.
items.notes: 'Retrieval can often be performed over multiple fields. For example, for scientific publication we have the title, the abstract, the document body, the authors list, and the journal name. So far we focused only on datasets that have one or two fields.'

items.summary: Author-stated limitation (Appendix B, item 5): BEIR benchmarks generalist retrieval models; specialized single-task models were not evaluated and can outperform generalist ones on their one task.
items.notes: 'In our benchmark, we focus on evaluating models that are able to generalize well for a broad range of retrieval tasks. Naturally in real-world, for some few tasks or domains, specialized models are available which can easily outperform generic models as they focus and perform well on a single task... Such task-specific models do not necessarily need to generalize across all diverse tasks.'

items.summary: Author-stated limitation (NeurIPS checklist item 3c): no error bars / seed variance are reported, because most evaluated systems are public pre-trained checkpoints without accessible training code, making re-training infeasible in many cases.
items.notes: '[No] We evaluate existing available pre-trained models that often come without suitable training code. Hence, in many cases, re-training the model is not feasible.'

items.summary: The TREC-COVID hole-filling annotation (Table 4 study) was performed by the paper's own authors, following the original TREC-COVID task's annotation guidelines, while blinded to which system had retrieved each missing judgment.
items.notes: 'During annotation, we were unaware of the system who retrieved the missing annotation to avoid a preference bias.' Checklist: 'We ourselves performed annotation on the TREC-COVID dataset... Annotations were done by the authors of the paper.'
